query: What signals suggest a travel expense will be declined?

per_column.name: asset_category
per_column.rationale: Categorises the expense type (hardware/travel/cloud etc.), well grounded in short_description and ci. Useful to isolate travel rows for the query, but is more of a routing dimension than a decline signal; moderate leverage.

per_column.name: expense_origin_method
per_column.rationale: Manual vs automated vs procurement origin is a plausible decline signal (manual entries may face more scrutiny). Grounded in phrasings like 'Automated' or 'Procurement of'; the procurement_request vs manual distinction is somewhat inferred but reasonable.

per_column.name: asset_action_type
per_column.rationale: Action taxonomy derivable from descriptions, but largely redundant with asset_category and expense_origin_method (e.g. registration_tracking tracks 'automated'). Modest new leverage.

per_column.name: source_id_present
per_column.rationale: Trivially derived boolean from existing source_id column; near-restatement of an original field, so low novelty. But missing source_id is a plausible decline signal, giving some usefulness. Fully grounded.

per_column.name: processing_lag_bucket
per_column.rationale: Buckets processed_date lag; 'not_processed' for nan is correct behaviour. Processing lag / not-yet-processed is a strong candidate signal for declines. Grounded in processed_date vs opened_at, though exact bucketing not fully verifiable from samples.

per_column.name: submitting_department
per_column.rationale: Largely redundant with the original 'department' column. Values look questionable: hardware/cloud rows attributed to Customer_Support and Sales with no supporting text in samples, suggesting the department is not actually readable from the shown source text.

per_column.name: vendor_brand
per_column.rationale: Extracts brand from ci (Dell, AWS, Samsonite). Well grounded and gives a genuine grouping axis; vendor could correlate with non-standard/declined expenses.

per_column.name: description_specificity
per_column.rationale: Distinguishes specific vs auto-generated vs placeholder descriptions, a reasonable proxy for scrutiny/decline risk. Grounded in description phrasing, though 'auto_generated_template' vs 'specific_model_named' boundary is judgment-based.

per_column.name: is_non_standard_item
per_column.rationale: Directly relevant: non-standard items are a classic decline trigger. However the derivation criteria are opaque and not clearly warranted by the sampled source text, lowering groundedness confidence.

per_column.name: hardware_asset_subtype
per_column.rationale: Reasonable subtype extraction (laptop/desktop) with correct NULL for non-hardware, but an AWS EC2 cloud service was labelled 'server' as a hardware subtype, a mislabel. Also tangential to a TRAVEL-expense decline query.

judge.rationale: The added columns provide several genuinely useful axes for predicting declines (origin method, processing lag, description specificity, non-standard flag, vendor), though a notable cluster is hardware-centric and tangential to the travel-expense focus of the query, and a few (source_id_present, submitting_department, asset_action_type) largely restate original columns or each other. Groundedness is generally sound with correct handling of missing values, but there are hallucination concerns: submitting_department values appear unsupported by the shown text, and a cloud service was mislabelled with a hardware 'server' subtype. Overall the set clears both necessary conditions moderately well.
